Notes from Underground is Dostoevsky's novella from 1864, and it presents the alienated voice of a former bureaucrat exposing what he sees as the bankruptcy of nineteenth-century rationalism and materialism. The protagonist is unnamed, defined only by isolation and wounded pride. Through bitter confession and recollection of humiliating social encounters, the Underground Man asserts the primacy of individual will, irrational desire, and suffering over utopian schemes premised on reason. He attacks the belief that humans are rational and perfectible, that society can be scientifically engineered toward happiness. Dostoevsky targets socialist and positivist ideals of his era, particularly the notion of a crystal palace of reason where human nature is calculable and malleable. The novella is structured in two parts. Part I is philosophical argument, and Part II recalls a humiliating night involving a prostitute and former schoolmates, illustrating the gap between theory and flesh. The Underground Man's insistence on the right to choose irrationally, to suffer, to assert his own will even destructively, presages existentialism and Nietzsche's will to power. Published in The Epoch, the novella's fragmented form and polemic intensity made it controversial and marginal for decades. But over time its reputation grew as psychological realism became a central literary concern. Today it is recognized as a modernist foundational text, a howl of protest against dehumanizing ideology that continues to reverberate through twentieth and twenty-first century thought.
